blocks.text: A red blood cell placed in distilled water swells and bursts, whereas a neurone keeps a steep sodium gradient even though sodium leaks in constantly. The same lipid bilayer is involved in both cases, so the real question is by which mechanism, and at what energy cost, each substance crosses.

blocks.markdown: The plasma membrane is selectively permeable. Small non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the lipid bilayer readily, whereas ions and polar solutes need membrane proteins. This unit compares **simple diffusion**, **facilitated diffusion** and **active transport**, then uses the Na+/K+-ATPase as the central example of how cells maintain ion gradients.

blocks.title: Core definitions
blocks.text: Simple diffusion is net movement of a solute down its concentration gradient directly through the lipid bilayer, with no protein and no energy input. Facilitated diffusion is movement down an electrochemical gradient through a specific membrane protein (a channel or a carrier) without direct energy input. Active transport is movement against an electrochemical gradient using energy: primary active transport uses ATP directly, and secondary active transport uses the energy stored in an ion gradient, usually sodium.

blocks.latex: \Delta G = RT \ln\!\left(\frac{C_{\text{in}}}{C_{\text{out}}}\right) \quad (\text{uncharged solute moved from outside to inside})
blocks.caption: Free energy to move one mole of an uncharged solute from outside to inside; R = 8.314 J per mol per K, T in kelvin
Nernst equation: the membrane potential at which ion X is at equilibrium (z is the ion's charge, F is Faraday's constant)

blocks.markdown: For ions the driving force is the **electrochemical gradient** (concentration plus voltage). Proteins do not change the thermodynamic direction of movement; they only provide a route. Carriers are **saturable**: rate rises with concentration and then plateaus at a maximum when all binding sites are occupied, whereas simple diffusion rises linearly with the gradient. Water crosses largely through **aquaporin** channels in cells that need high water permeability, such as the renal collecting duct and the erythrocyte, which is facilitated diffusion.

blocks.title: Classifying transport processes
blocks.prompt: Classify (i) oxygen crossing an alveolar cell membrane, (ii) glucose uptake into an erythrocyte through GLUT1, (iii) sodium export by the Na+/K+-ATPase, (iv) sodium-glucose cotransport (SGLT1) across the apical membrane of an enterocyte.

steps.text: Oxygen is small and non-polar, so it dissolves in the bilayer and moves down its gradient: simple diffusion.
GLUT1 is a carrier that moves glucose down its gradient without ATP: facilitated diffusion.
The Na+/K+-ATPase uses ATP to pump sodium out against its electrochemical gradient: primary active transport.
SGLT1 uses the inward sodium gradient to import glucose uphill: secondary active transport (symport).

blocks.answer: (i) simple diffusion; (ii) facilitated diffusion; (iii) primary active transport; (iv) secondary active transport.

rows: Uphill for one solute, driven by downhill sodium
Carriers yes; channels show a limit
blocks.caption: Comparison of membrane transport mechanisms

blocks.markdown: **The Na+/K+-ATPase.** Each cycle uses one ATP to export 3 Na+ and import 2 K+, so it is **electrogenic** (one net positive charge leaves per cycle), contributing a small direct negative shift to the resting potential. Its main roles are to keep intracellular Na+ low and K+ high, which sets up the gradients for K+ leak channels to create most of the resting potential of about -70 mV in many cells, and to keep cell volume stable: without it, accumulating intracellular solute would draw water in and the cell would swell. Cardiac glycosides such as digoxin and ouabain inhibit the pump (a pharmacology example), so intracellular Na+ rises.

blocks.title: Why a pump inhibitor stops glucose absorption
blocks.prompt: An enterocyte's basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase is inhibited. Predict the effect on apical SGLT1-mediated glucose uptake.

steps.text: Without the pump, intracellular Na+ rises and the inward Na+ gradient dissipates.
SGLT1 relies on that gradient to drive glucose uphill, so uptake falls.
ATP is still not hydrolysed by SGLT1 itself, yet the process depends on it indirectly.

blocks.answer: Glucose uptake falls because the sodium gradient that powers SGLT1 collapses.

items: Symport moves both solutes in the same direction (SGLT1); antiport moves them in opposite directions (Na+/Ca2+ exchanger).
Secondary transporters do not hydrolyse ATP but depend on the gradient the Na+/K+-ATPase maintains.
A protein-mediated route does not make transport active; direction and energy source do.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A channel speeds transport but does not make it active. If a solute moves down its electrochemical gradient through a protein, it is facilitated diffusion.

points: Simple diffusion crosses the lipid bilayer without protein or energy; facilitated diffusion uses channels or carriers but is still downhill.
The Na+/K+-ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP, maintaining ion gradients and cell volume, and is electrogenic.
Secondary active transport (symport, antiport) uses the sodium gradient, so it depends indirectly on ATP; the Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential of an ion.

questions.stem: Water moves rapidly across the membrane of a renal collecting duct cell through protein channels, down its osmotic gradient and without ATP. How is this transport classified?

options.text: Facilitated diffusion
Simple diffusion
Primary active transport
Secondary active transport

distractorRationale.b: Simple diffusion does not use a protein.
distractorRationale.c: No ATP is used and the movement is downhill.
distractorRationale.d: No coupled ion gradient is used.

questions.explanation: A protein channel (aquaporin) provides the route, and the movement follows the gradient with no energy input. This is the definition of facilitated diffusion.

questions.stem: Which substance crosses an alveolar cell membrane mainly by simple diffusion?

options.text: Carbon dioxide
Sodium ions
Glucose
Amino acids

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is small and non-polar and dissolves in the lipid bilayer. Charged and polar solutes need membrane proteins.

questions.stem: A cardiac glycoside inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase of a myocyte. What is the most direct immediate change?

options.text: Intracellular Na+ rises and the sodium and potassium gradients decline
Intracellular K+ rises above its normal level
The membrane becomes more permeable to oxygen
Aquaporins stop working

questions.correctOptionText: Intracellular Na+ rises and the sodium and potassium gradients decline

distractorRationale.b: K+ import falls so intracellular K+ declines.
distractorRationale.c: Oxygen crosses by simple diffusion unaffected.
distractorRationale.d: Aquaporins do not depend on the pump.

questions.explanation: The pump continuously exports Na+ against leak. Inhibiting it lets Na+ accumulate and gradients decay, and this also reduces the driving force for sodium-coupled transporters.

questions.stem: In a proximal tubule cell, amino acid uptake through a Na+-coupled symporter falls when the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase is blocked. Why?

options.text: The sodium gradient that drives the symporter dissipates
The symporter directly hydrolyses ATP made by the pump
The amino acid can no longer diffuse through the lipid bilayer
Aquaporins block amino acid entry

questions.correctOptionText: The sodium gradient that drives the symporter dissipates

distractorRationale.b: Secondary transporters do not hydrolyse ATP.
distractorRationale.c: Amino acids cannot cross the bilayer by simple diffusion in the first place.

questions.explanation: A symporter uses the energy of downhill sodium movement. When the pump fails, the inward sodium gradient collapses and uphill amino acid uptake falls.

questions.stem: An experiment shows that uptake of solute X rises in proportion to its external concentration without limit, while uptake of solute Y rises and then plateaus. What can be inferred?

options.text: X crosses by simple diffusion and Y uses a saturable carrier
X uses a saturable carrier and Y crosses by simple diffusion
Both use the Na+/K+-ATPase
Both are actively transported

questions.correctOptionText: X crosses by simple diffusion and Y uses a saturable carrier

distractorRationale.c: The pump transports only Na+ and K+.
distractorRationale.d: Plateau alone does not show active transport.

questions.explanation: Linear uptake with no maximum is typical of simple diffusion, and a plateau reflects a finite number of carrier binding sites. A plateau does not by itself show the movement is uphill.

questions.stem: At 310 K, a cell accumulates an uncharged solute to an internal concentration 100 times higher than outside. Using delta G = RT ln(Cin/Cout) with R = 8.314 J per mol per K, calculate the minimum free energy needed to move one mole into the cell, in kilojoules per mole.
questions.explanation: delta G = 8.314 x 310 x ln(100) = 8.314 x 310 x 4.605 = 11,869 J per mole, or 11.87 kJ per mole. This is positive, showing uphill transport needs an energy input such as ATP hydrolysis or an ion gradient.

questions.stem: A cell has [K+] of 5 mM outside and 150 mM inside. Using the Nernst equation with 61.5 mV per log10 unit at 37 degrees Celsius and z = +1, calculate the potassium equilibrium potential in millivolts.
questions.explanation: E = 61.5 x log10(5/150) = 61.5 x log10(0.0333) = 61.5 x (-1.477) = -90.8 mV. The steep K+ gradient, established by the Na+/K+-ATPase, is why a K+-permeable resting membrane is negative inside.

questions.stem: Compare simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and primary active transport in terms of energy source, direction relative to the gradient and the role of membrane proteins.
markingGuide: Simple diffusion: through the lipid bilayer, no protein, down the gradient, no energy input.
Facilitated diffusion: through a channel or carrier, still down the electrochemical gradient, no direct ATP.
Primary active transport: pump uses direct ATP hydrolysis and can move solute against its gradient.
Proteins change the route, not the thermodynamic direction, unless energy is supplied.
Carrier and pump processes are saturable.
questions.explanation: The key is separating route from energy. Only active transport supplies energy to move a solute uphill.

questions.stem: Explain how the Na+/K+-ATPase generates and maintains the ion gradients of an animal cell, why it is electrogenic, and why it also protects against cell swelling.
markingGuide: Uses ATP hydrolysis; exports 3 Na+ and imports 2 K+ per cycle.
Maintains low intracellular Na+ and high intracellular K+ against leak.
Electrogenic: net one positive charge out per cycle, contributing to a negative inside.
Gradients and K+ leak set the resting potential.
Exporting Na+ stops intracellular solute accumulating and drawing water in, so cell volume is preserved.
questions.explanation: A complete answer links stoichiometry to gradients, potential and volume control.

questions.stem: Explain how secondary active transport couples to the sodium gradient. Distinguish symport from antiport using one example of each, and explain why the process still depends indirectly on ATP.
markingGuide: Sodium moves down its electrochemical gradient through the transporter, and the released energy drives another solute uphill.
Symport moves both in the same direction, e.g. SGLT1 for glucose.
Antiport moves them in opposite directions, e.g. the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger.
The transporter does not hydrolyse ATP, but the Na+/K+-ATPase creates and maintains the sodium gradient.
questions.explanation: The sodium gradient is the stored energy source. The pump sets it up using ATP, so the coupling is indirect.

questions.stem: Which description fits secondary active transport?

options.text: A transporter uses the energy of an ion gradient to move another solute uphill
A carrier hydrolyses ATP to move a solute uphill
A solute dissolves in the bilayer and moves downhill
A channel opens and ions flow downhill

questions.correctOptionText: A transporter uses the energy of an ion gradient to move another solute uphill
questions.explanation: Secondary active transporters couple downhill ion movement to uphill solute movement. They depend on the gradient built by primary active pumps.

questions.stem: In cardiac muscle, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger moves 3 Na+ into the cell as it moves 1 Ca2+ out. How is it classified?

options.text: Secondary active transport by an antiporter
Secondary active transport by a symporter
Primary active transport by an ATPase
Facilitated diffusion by a channel

questions.correctOptionText: Secondary active transport by an antiporter

distractorRationale.a: Correct: opposite directions, uses the Na+ gradient.
distractorRationale.b: The solutes move in opposite directions.
distractorRationale.c: The exchanger does not hydrolyse ATP.

questions.explanation: Sodium moving in down its gradient drives calcium out against its gradient. Because the two ions move in opposite directions, the exchanger is an antiporter.
